one_line: Pencil.dev design-to-code workflow with Claude Code: a file-watcher syncs .pen edits to code, subagents build pages, and a UX-audit skill raised the site grade from C to B.
summary: AI LABS describes a small team's attempt to close the design-to-code gap using Pencil.dev, a design canvas that connects to Claude Code over MCP and stores designs as a JSON .pen file inside the project repo. Sync was not automatic, so the team wrote a watcher script that fires the Claude CLI with a sync prompt on each save, with a cooldown to limit token burn. Unattended runs need permissions pre-configured in the .claude settings, or Claude stalls on a permission prompt. For a multi-page build, Claude Code spawned one agent per page (five pages), grounded in PRD and UI-guide docs kept in the repo. Motion was added with GSAP using XML-structured prompts, and Lenis was layered on for smooth scrolling. Finally, a UX Audit skill built with Skill Creator (nine-point checklist, Python checks, scored report) graded the site C, the fixes addressed two critical issues (mostly color contrast), and the re-run graded it B. It is a practical walkthrough, but the watcher script and prompts are paywalled and no code, costs or benchmarks are shown.

key_ideas.idea: Design-to-code is still broken: prompt-to-code tools have no editable canvas, and the Figma MCP is read-only, so every design change means reprompting from scratch.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker positions Pencil.dev as a bidirectional bridge between a design canvas and a coding agent, which is the gap the team wanted closed.

key_ideas.idea: Pencil.dev's desktop app auto-configures its MCP in Claude Code, and designs are stored as a JSON .pen file in the project folder that Git can track.
key_ideas.detail: Opus 4.6 was used; all OpenAI and Anthropic models showed up in the chat. Pencil uses coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex under the hood.

key_ideas.idea: The bridge does not auto-sync in either direction. Each design change had to be pushed to code with a manual prompt, which the team found too much overhead.
key_ideas.detail: Claude analyzed the design section by section and rebuilt it as HTML, matching the canvas exactly, but repeating that after every edit was impractical.

key_ideas.idea: A watcher script closes the loop: it monitors the .pen file and fires the Claude CLI with a sync prompt on save, with a cooldown so rapid saves do not trigger repeated runs.
key_ideas.detail: Started with an npm run sync command. The cooldown means small rapid edits are not synced individually, trading immediacy for fewer token-burning runs.

key_ideas.idea: Unattended automation needs permissions pre-configured in the project's .claude settings (read, write and MCP tool calls). Without them Claude blocks indefinitely on a permission prompt.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker calls this a required pre-step before the watcher is useful.

key_ideas.idea: For multi-page work, Claude Code can spawn parallel subagents, each owning one page of the app, using the PRD and UI guide already stored as repo docs as shared context.
key_ideas.detail: Five pages produced five agents. The resulting pages kept the same fonts and styling as the landing page, and the watcher then implemented the design in the app.

key_ideas.idea: Motion was added with GSAP driven by a long XML-structured prompt that lists task, dependencies, notes and per-element behavior in tags. The speaker says Claude responds better to XML.
key_ideas.detail: The XML prompt approach was reused for the next step, the Lenis change. The speaker says the prompts are in the paid community.

key_ideas.idea: GSAP and Lenis are layered, not redundant: GSAP decides what happens on scroll, while Lenis (smooth scroll) controls how the scroll feels, so GSAP triggers look more natural.
key_ideas.detail: Lenis was added on top of the GSAP setup in a second XML-prompted pass that changed multiple parts of the repo.

key_ideas.idea: A UX Audit skill made with Skill Creator runs phases (gather context, check against a nine-point UX checklist, score and report), with Python scripts that catch issues programmatically.
key_ideas.detail: First audit: letter grade C, two critical issues (color contrast) plus major and minor ones. The team asked Claude to implement the fixes and re-ran the audit, which improved the grade to B. The speaker claims WCAG compliance improved, with no measurement shown.

techniques.name: Design file as a repo artifact
techniques.how: Install the Pencil.dev desktop app, let it auto-configure its MCP for Claude Code, and design on the canvas. The design is saved as a .pen JSON file in the project folder, so it can be committed to Git and versioned alongside the code.
techniques.when: When designers and coding agents must share one source of truth and you want the design versioned like code.

techniques.name: Save-triggered sync watcher
techniques.how: A Node/npm script (run with npm run sync) uses JS file-watching libraries to monitor the .pen file. On each save it invokes the claude CLI with a fixed sync prompt that says how to map the design onto the project. A cooldown period between triggers stops repeated runs. The speaker shows no code; the script is in the paid community.
techniques.when: When you iterate on a design many times and do not want to reprompt the agent after each change. Set the cooldown high enough to avoid token burn and session limits.

techniques.name: Pre-approve permissions for unattended claude runs
techniques.how: Before running a headless or watcher-driven claude session, add the needed permissions (read, write, and the MCP tool calls) to the project's .claude/settings.json. The speaker names the file but shows no keys.
techniques.when: Any automated run where no human is present to answer permission prompts. Without it the run blocks forever.

techniques.name: One subagent per page with shared docs
techniques.how: Keep PRD and UI-guide docs in the repo. Prompt Claude Code to split the work by page, e.g. explicitly tell it to give each agent one aspect, and it spawns one agent per page. Each agent reads the shared docs and the design via the MCP tools.
techniques.when: Building several similar pages in parallel where each page can be built independently and must match a common style.

techniques.name: XML-tagged task prompts
techniques.how: Write each implementation prompt in XML tags: task details, dependencies, important notes, and a block per target element describing its exact behavior, plus rules at the end. The speaker says this is for Claude's parsing.
techniques.when: Detailed, multi-element UI changes such as adding motion, where you want each element's behavior specified precisely.

techniques.name: Layer Lenis over GSAP for scroll
techniques.how: Use GSAP for scroll-triggered animations and add Lenis (open-source smooth scroll) on top for the scroll feel. Prompt the agent with the dependencies and the element-level placement and behavior, as in the GSAP step.
techniques.when: Scroll-driven landing pages where jumpy native scrolling makes GSAP triggers feel abrupt.

techniques.name: UX Audit skill with a scored re-run loop
techniques.how: Create the skill with Skill Creator. Phases: gather context, analyze the nine-point UX checklist (kept in a reference file), run the Python checks, then report a letter grade with issues ranked critical, major and minor. Ask the agent to fix the issues and re-run the audit to confirm the grade moved (the talk shows C to B).
techniques.when: Before calling a UI done, to catch accessibility and usability issues such as contrast that a human eye may miss.

numbers.claim: Five pages were built by five parallel Claude Code agents, one per page.
Model used: Opus 4.6 (all OpenAI and Anthropic models were available in the chat).
UX checklist has nine points. The first audit graded the site C with two critical issues (color contrast) plus major and minor ones; after fixes the re-run graded it B.
The watcher uses a cooldown between triggers, but no duration is given.
No token counts, costs, latencies or benchmarks are given.

hot_takes: The bidirectional-bridge pitch is overstated: sync is manual by default, and the team had to build a watcher to get near-automatic behavior.
The core automation (watcher script, sync prompts, GSAP and XML prompts, UX audit skill) is sold through the channel's paid AI LABS Pro community, so the reusable parts are not shown.
The XML claim ('Claude models are explicitly tuned for XML') is asserted, not tested in the video.
The UX grade and the WCAG-compliance claim come from one self-run audit with no method or before/after metrics shown.
Tool is described as free at the time of recording (1:13), but the video does not say how the desktop app and MCP connect beyond local install.

relevance.why: Wraps the claude CLI in a file-watch loop with cooldown and pre-approved permissions, similar to ProsHarness loops/schedules. The unattended permission-prompt stall is a failure mode to guard against.
relevance.action: Compare the watcher's cooldown and pre-approved permissions in .claude/settings.json with ProsHarness loops/schedules, and add a test that an unattended claude run fails fast on a permission prompt instead of hanging.

relevance.why: One subagent per page with shared PRD/UI docs is a concrete split-and-parallelize pattern for multi-agent coding, and the UX-audit skill with a re-run loop is a reusable verification pattern.
relevance.action: Try a multi-agent split (one agent per independent module, each reading shared spec docs in the repo) on a small task, and measure whether it beats a single agent.
